headline: Self-Hosting AI Models Cost $500 in 3 Months, APIs cost $1.50 for same workload
summary: An engineer spent $500 over three months trying to self-host LLMs, facing crashes and slow speeds. They switched to an API that costs under $2/month for the same workload, offering better reliability and performance.
details: A developer invested $500 on GPU rental over three months, attempting to self-host various LLMs like Llama 2 and Mixtral. Despite having a spare RTX 3090, they struggled with Docker, CUDA versions, and VRAM limits, failing to achieve reliable model operation.

The actual costs quickly escalated beyond the initial setup. Renting cloud GPUs for larger models, such as Llama 2 70B, required multi-GPU instances at about $3.50 per hour for an A100. Even a 13B model on a local 3090 was slow, generating only 10 tokens per second, while the 70B model frequently crashed.

The developer ultimately transitioned to an API solution, drastically cutting costs. For a workload of 100,000 tokens per month, self-hosting amounted to around $100, whereas the API cost approximately $1.50. API requests also returned in under a second, eliminating the need for GPU management or debugging VRAM issues.

Performance and quality were also significant factors. Proprietary APIs like OpenAI's GPT-4o-mini can generate over 100 tokens per second, far surpassing the 20 tokens per second achieved by a 13B model on a 3090. Open-source models, while improving, still lag behind top proprietary models in reasoning, instruction following, and factual accuracy for production applications.

While self-hosting has niche applications, such as handling highly sensitive data, specific fine-tuning, or offline requirements, it is generally not optimal for most developers. For common tasks like building chatbots, code assistants, or internal tools, APIs offer a superior balance of cost, speed, and reliability.

The switch to an API freed the developer to concentrate on building features rather than managing infrastructure. Using a unified API provider allowed access to multiple models (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini) through a single endpoint, addressing concerns about vendor lock-in and simplifying model switching.

headline_marked: [[AI assistants prove their worth]] by streamlining business card follow-ups
headline: AI assistants prove their worth by streamlining business card follow-ups
summary: A developer initially skeptical of AI assistants found them indispensable for a tedious post-networking task, automating personalized email drafts from a stack of business cards.
details: The author initially dismissed AI assistants, seeing no practical use beyond trivial tasks like deciding who drives kids. They believed one-off AI subscriptions were sufficient for their needs.
This changed after a business event where they collected numerous business cards. The daunting task of sending personalized follow-up emails to each contact highlighted a clear need for assistance.
Manually, this process involved tedious steps: typing email addresses, composing messages, and reviewing each one carefully. The thought alone was time-consuming and prone to errors.

Using a coding agent, the author simply photographed all cards, instructed the AI to extract contact details, and then to draft personalized emails. The AI created drafts for review, which were then sent automatically.

This experience felt like interacting with a real assistant, handling tasks through voice commands without navigating complex UIs. It solidified the author's belief in the practical utility of AI assistants for streamlining repetitive tasks.
